stem: Several months after an axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, a client reports that the affected-side arm feels newly heavy and tight and that a bracelet has become noticeably tighter. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess and compare the arms for swelling and other changes and promptly refer the client for evaluation of possible early lymphedema.
options.B: Reassure the client that heaviness and tightness are expected after axillary surgery and require evaluation only if the arm doubles in size.
options.C: Encourage immediate heavy resistance exercise with the affected arm to force lymphatic drainage before any assessment is performed.
options.D: Assume the symptoms confirm lymphedema and begin unsupervised tight compression wrapping without evaluating other causes of arm swelling.

rationale: Axillary lymph node dissection increases the risk of breast cancer-related lymphedema. NCI advises clients to watch for even slight changes such as heaviness, fullness, tightness, swelling, weakness, or tighter-fitting clothing or jewelry and to report them for evaluation. Assessment can include comparison of limb size and, when indicated, tests that help distinguish lymphedema from other causes of swelling such as venous thrombosis or infection. Early symptoms should not be dismissed, but they also do not establish the diagnosis by themselves. Exercise is generally safe and may support lymph flow when individualized, but new symptoms should be assessed before an unsupervised high-intensity program or compression treatment is started.
educational_objective: Recognize subtle early signs of upper-extremity lymphedema after axillary lymph node dissection and prioritize prompt assessment while avoiding outdated blanket precautions or unassessed self-treatment.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health

source_locator: Lymphedema and Cancer — What are symptoms of lymphedema? and How is lymphedema diagnosed?; Health Professional PDQ — Breast Cancer risk factors and Physical exercise
source_claim_supported: NCI identifies axillary lymph node dissection as a risk factor for breast cancer-related lymphedema and lists new heaviness, tightness, swelling, weakness, and tighter clothing/jewelry as warning signs that should be reported and evaluated. NCI notes that other causes of limb swelling should be considered and that exercise has not been shown to be inherently harmful when appropriately used.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

correction_summary: Completely rebuilt the original blanket-prevention item. Removed the overbroad rule that every arm merely at risk after axillary lymph node dissection must universally avoid all blood pressure measurements and injections; NCI specifically gives contralateral-arm BP/blood-draw advice for an arm with established lymphedema. The final item instead tests NCI-supported early symptom recognition, prompt evaluation, differential assessment, and safe avoidance of unassessed high-intensity exercise or compression. Remapped from Basic Care and Comfort to Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings: Original item stated broad arm restrictions after axillary node dissection as if they were universally evidence-based prevention requirements for every at-risk arm.
Fresh NCI review distinguishes risk after axillary dissection from management of an arm with established lymphedema and emphasizes early symptom recognition and assessment.
The final stem uses subtle NCI-listed warning signs—heaviness, tightness, and tighter jewelry—rather than waiting for advanced swelling.
Diagnostic certainty is avoided because venous thrombosis, infection, malignancy, and other causes of swelling may require exclusion.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct priority action with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, outdated blanket precaution, or unresolved source conflict.
